theme: Wikipedia pageviews tooling and destination-demand datasets (pageviews for cities/attractions as tourism proxies)
queries_run: gh search repos "wikipedia pageviews api" --sort stars
gh search repos "tourism demand nowcasting" --sort stars
gh search repos "wikipedia trends forecasting travel" --sort stars
gh search repos "attraction visitor pageviews" --sort stars
gh search repos "wikipedia pageviews tourism" --sort stars

candidates.name: AUS-Wiki-Binder
candidates.what_it_holds: R scripts (Fixed-origin-Wiki.R 28KB, Fixed-origin-tourism.R 36KB, OLSmodel_se.R) implementing 'fast forecast reconciliation using linear models' that pairs Australian official tourism statistics with Wikipedia pageviews as a covariate/predictor, wrapped for Binder/RStudio interactive use. No raw data files committed (scripts pull tourism + Wikipedia series at run time); academic methodology repo (mahsaashouri appears to be a forecast-reconciliation researcher, likely tied to a published paper).
candidates.why_useful: Directly on-theme: a working academic method that uses Wikipedia pageviews to nowcast/forecast a country's tourism demand, with real code (not just a notebook). Fills part of gap #5 (Wikipedia pageviews tooling) and is a template method for using pageviews as an APAC travel-demand proxy (gap #7, Australia). Worth reading the underlying paper for the reconciliation approach even though it targets AUS not US/EMEA.
candidates.time_coverage: unspecified (README/short; scripts likely span whatever the source tourism series covers)
candidates.size_hint: ~65KB of R scripts, no data files
candidates.last_activity: unspecified (repo appears stable/older; not a 2026 update per search metadata ordering)

candidates.name: nz-attraction-pageviews
candidates.what_it_holds: Python/DuckDB pipeline that incrementally ingests DAILY Wikipedia pageviews (Wikimedia Analytics API, per-article all-access user pageviews, CC0) for eight named New Zealand tourist-attraction Wikipedia articles (e.g. Milford Sound) into a local warehouse.duckdb, with retry/backfill logic, watermark tracking, and a venues CSV listing the monitored attractions. No raw pageview data or database file is committed to the repo itself — it is a one-command pull tool, not a dataset.
candidates.why_useful: A clean, small, working example of exactly the tooling class named in gap #5 ('Wikipedia pageviews tooling') and gap #20 (destination/attraction proxies) — could be forked/adapted in under a day to pull daily pageviews for Airbnb-relevant destination Wikipedia pages (e.g. specific cities/neighborhoods, FIFA World Cup host-city pages for gap #11) as a free, near-real-time tourism-interest proxy, unlike Google Trends which the team already found not point-in-time/renormalized and failing (per CONTEXT.md 'ideas tested and found not to work').
candidates.time_coverage: daily ingestion; demo shows 90-day backfill default, live example spans 7 days at time of README
candidates.size_hint: small codebase; DuckDB warehouse built at runtime, not committed

candidates.name: pageview-api
candidates.what_it_holds: Mature Python client (31 stars, actively updated to Aug 2026) for the official Wikimedia Pageview REST API (per-article, per-project, per-country pageview counts, various access/agent breakdowns). No data committed; it is a well-maintained API wrapper.
candidates.why_useful: The most robust, still-maintained Python client for pulling Wikipedia pageviews for any set of city/attraction/company articles going back to mid-2015 (official Wikimedia pageviews dataset start). Fills gap #5 tooling need with a production-quality option rather than a one-off script; could pull ABNB-relevant destination-city pageviews, or even the 'Airbnb' company article itself, as an engagement/interest proxy.
candidates.time_coverage: Wikimedia pageviews API covers ~July 2015 to present at daily/monthly/hourly granularity

candidates.name: pageviews (Ironholds)
candidates.what_it_holds: R client library (24 stars) for the Wikimedia pageview API, from a long-time Wikimedia data engineer; wraps the same REST API as Commonists' Python client but for R users.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative-language (R) tooling for the same pageviews-as-proxy approach; useful if the team's stats work is in R rather than Python. Same use case as Commonists/pageview-api.

candidates.name: pageviews.js
candidates.what_it_holds: JavaScript/Node client (27 stars) for the Wikimedia Pageviews API, usable in browser or Node.js.
candidates.why_useful: Another mature client if any tooling needs to run in a JS/Node context (e.g. a dashboard); same underlying data source as the Python/R clients above.

candidates.name: pageviews (Wikimedia Foundation tool)
candidates.what_it_holds: The official-ish, actively maintained (164 stars, updated Sep 2026) Pageviews Analysis web tool used on Wikimedia Toolforge, source code for pageviews.wmcloud.org / pageviews.toolforge.org — lets you compare pageview trends across articles/projects/date ranges interactively, and its underlying code can be adapted to bulk-pull series.
candidates.why_useful: Highest-star, best-maintained pageviews tool found in this sweep; even if used only as the live web tool (not cloned), it is the fastest manual way to eyeball a city or attraction's Wikipedia interest trend as a sanity check on other tourism-demand proxies. Its source also documents the API request shape most robustly.
candidates.size_hint: web app source, no bundled long time series

candidates.name: pvduck
candidates.what_it_holds: Tool to aggregate raw Wikimedia pageviews DUMP files (the https://dumps.wikimedia.org/other/pageviews/ hourly dumps, not the aggregated REST API) directly into a DuckDB database, letting you query pageviews at scale without downloading/parsing gzipped dump files by hand.
candidates.why_useful: Useful complementary tool to gap #5: the raw dumps go back further and are finer-grained (hourly, all-article) than the REST API's per-article convenience endpoint, so pvduck is the practical way to mine that firehose for a specific set of destination-city articles across years without standing up Hadoop/Spark.
candidates.time_coverage: Wikimedia pageview dumps span 2015-present (hourly raw counts)
candidates.size_hint: small tool; user supplies which dump files to ingest

candidates.name: wiki-download-parse-page-views
candidates.what_it_holds: Pipeline (from GESIS, a European social-science research institute) for downloading, parsing, and aggregating the static Wikipedia pageview dumps at scale; academic/research-grade tooling, actively updated (Jun 2026).
candidates.why_useful: Another route into the historical raw pageview dumps (2015-present) with an academic-institution maintenance track record, useful as a backup/cross-check to pvduck for building a multi-year destination-pageviews panel.

candidates.name: WhereInTheWorldIsWikipedia
candidates.what_it_holds: Wikimedia Research team code for geographically mapping Wikimedia pageviews (i.e. attributing pageviews to reader geography/country), not article-topic geography.
candidates.why_useful: Marginal: could in principle help split 'reader interest by country' for a destination article, which is a weaker but distinct signal (who is searching about a place) versus 'interest in a place.' Not a ready dataset.
candidates.time_coverage: unspecified, likely historical Wikimedia research-era (repo appears older/low-activity)

candidates.name: waxer
candidates.what_it_holds: Official Wikimedia Foundation R client for the Wikimedia Analytics Query Service (AQS) API, the same backend the pageviews REST API sits on; actively updated (Jul 2026).
candidates.why_useful: Official, currently-maintained alternative to Commonists/Ironholds for R users wanting AQS/pageviews data; broader than pure pageviews (also edits, unique devices) which could proxy general public attention to a destination or to Airbnb itself.

candidates.name: us-attention-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Cross-platform 'attention tracking' dataset combining Wikipedia pageviews, GDELT events, and Google Trends, described as covering 2025 weekly data.
candidates.why_useful: If it includes travel/tourism/company-topic pageview series with committed CSVs, it's a ready-made multi-source attention panel; GDELT + pageviews + Trends together could triangulate consumer/travel sentiment shifts (gap #14/#5), though team's own testing found Trends-as-pulled fails, so value hinges on the pageviews component specifically. Not verified further (only description read, not repo contents).

candidates.name: influenza-wikipedia-dataset
candidates.what_it_holds: Committed dataset pairing official influenza incidence records with Wikipedia pagecounts/pageviews for flu-related articles, used in epidemiological nowcasting research.
candidates.why_useful: Not travel-relevant directly, but it is a concrete, committed example of the exact methodology pattern (pageviews as a leading/coincident indicator for a real-world demand series, validated against ground truth) that the team could replicate for tourism articles — useful as a methods reference for gap #17 (nowcasting with mixed-frequency data) even though the topic is epidemiology.
candidates.geography: not specified (likely Italy/EU given fluTN org name)

candidates.name: statsgrokse
candidates.what_it_holds: R binding to the legacy stats.grok.se service providing Wikipedia pageview statistics for 2008 through 2015 — i.e. pre-dating the official Wikimedia pageviews API/dumps (which start July 2015).
candidates.why_useful: The only tool found in this sweep that reaches PRE-2015 Wikipedia pageview history, which is otherwise unavailable from the official API/dumps. Low relevance to ABNB itself (founded 2008, IPO 2020) but could extend a destination-interest panel a few years further back than any other pageviews source, or serve pre-2015 case studies of other travel/kernel businesses.
candidates.time_coverage: 2008-2015 (fills the gap before official Wikimedia pageviews dumps begin)
candidates.size_hint: small R package, no bundled data

candidates.name: wikipedia-decline-llm
candidates.what_it_holds: Uses the Wikimedia Pageviews API to estimate Wikipedia traffic decline attributable to AI chatbots (LLM referral cannibalization).
candidates.why_useful: Off-theme for tourism demand but directly relevant to gap #19 (AI-referral traffic / bot-share datasets) — same pageviews API, different application: could be adapted to check whether AI-chatbot-driven decline in Wikipedia/travel-site traffic is a confound for any web-engagement-based tourism proxy the team builds.

notes: Theme is narrow and the GitHub search surface is dominated by generic tutorial/ETL-pipeline repos (Airflow/Spark/dbt pageview pipelines for tech-company or election topics, none holding travel data) which were excluded per instructions. No repo found holds a committed, ready-to-use PANEL of destination/attraction pageviews already joined to ABNB-relevant geographies (the two most promising, AUS-Wiki-Binder and nz-attraction-pageviews, are both methods/scripts that pull data at runtime rather than shipped datasets) -- so this theme is best read as 'tooling exists, someone still has to run it against a chosen list of destination/FIFA-host-city/competitor-brand Wikipedia articles.' No topic tag 'wikipedia-pageviews' or 'tourism-forecasting' returned useful hits via --topic search (topic=pageviews was dominated by generic web-analytics SDKs, not Wikipedia-specific). Did not find anything for 'pageviews tourism forecasting' combined query (0 results) or 'wikipedia pageviews tourism' combined (0 results) -- the useful hits all came from single-concept queries ('wikimedia pageviews', 'wikipedia pageviews') scanned manually for travel relevance. Used all 6 permitted gh search repos calls; did not touch gh search code. Recommend a follow-on scout specifically build the small pull script (using Commonists/pageview-api or the raw MusikAnimal tool) against a hand-picked list of Airbnb top-market cities/FIFA host cities rather than searching further -- the ceiling here is a method, not a dataset, and the team already has a negative-result precedent with Google Trends for this class of engagement proxy, so expectations should be modest (medium potential at best, contingent on out-of-sample validation the team has not yet run).
